Autonomous robots operating in open and changing environments must adapt not only what they know, but also how they think, learn, and interact when previously unseen situations arise. However, most existing approaches assume predefined reasoning, learning, or interaction mechanisms and mainly adapt knowledge or model parameters within these fixed structures. This paper proposes an open-ended cognitive evolution framework that maintains a minimal cognitive core while allowing concrete thinking, learning, and interaction methods to be selected, validated, reused, updated, and expanded according to observed evidence and accumulated experience. The framework also incorporates discrepancy-driven evaluation to detect when previously valid knowledge or capabilities have become outdated. Experiments over five independent seeds show that newly acquired thinking activities achieve 94.67% first-encounter success on unseen conflict families, with 98.67% reuse. Adaptive learning-method selection reaches 95.00% accuracy and improves task success to 69.16%, compared with 55.66% for the best fixed learner. Under unannounced environmental changes, the proposed method achieves 96.43% task success, only 1.07% hazard rate and 1.43% outdated decisions, while reducing verification operations by 48.0% relative to periodic updating.

Autonomous robots operating in open and changing environments must adapt not only what they know, but also how they think, learn, and interact when previously unseen situations arise. \", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10783119/v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 8, 31]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.33612/diss.1528523889\", \"title\": [\"Open-Ended Interactive Robot Learning in Human-Centered Environments\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.33612/diss.1528523889\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.31219/osf.io/vgbh6\", \"title\": [\"Utilizing Foundation Models to Enhance Autonomous Robotic Systems in Dynamic and Unstructured Environments\"], \"abstract\": \"

Autonomous robotics in unstructured environments,such as disaster zones and construction sites, presents significantchallenges due to unpredictability and complexity. Traditionalrobotic systems often struggle with adaptability and generalization in these settings. Recent advancements in foundationmodels, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and LargeVision Models (LVMs), offer promising solutions by enhancingperception, decision-making, and interaction capabilities. Thispaper explores the integration of foundation models into autonomous robotics, systematically reviewing current applications,identifying challenges, and proposing future research directions.We analyze the impact of these models on various robotic tasks,assess the current level of autonomy achieved, and envisionscenarios for fully autonomous operations. Our findings indicatethat while foundation models significantly improve cognitivetasks, their application in physical interactions remains nascent.This study serves as a comprehensive benchmark for futureadvancements in autonomous robotics within dynamic and unstructured environments
